newsitem.title: USA: Senate votes expanded probe of fundraising.
newsitem.headline: Senate votes expanded probe of fundraising.

text.p: The Senate voted on Tuesday for a sweeping investigation into campaign fund-raising abuses after Republican leaders backed down from demands for a limited probe of only illegal activities.

After lengthy negotiations among Republicans who control the Senate and the minority Democrats, the Senate agreed to a deal to expand the probe from only illegal fund raising to both "illegal and improper" activities.

The plan to expand the probe was approved on a 99 to 0 vote on an amendment to a measure that would authorise spending $4.35 million to look into fund-raising irregularities, with the focus on foreign donations to Democrats for President Bill Clinton's 1996 campaign.
The Senate later voted by the same margin for the funding of the investigation.
Democrats voiced surprise and satisfaction at the sudden ourtcome of the debate.

"This was a victory today for those who want campaign reform in both parties," said Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, the top Democrat on the Governmental Affairs Committee, which is to carry out the investigation.
He said the Republican position of opposing the wider investigation had been "basically untenable."
The votes ended weeks of a stalemate and arguments between Republicans and Democrats over the scope of the investigation.

Sen. Christopher Dodd, a Connecticut Democrat who was general chairman last year of the Democratic National Committee, the party's administrative and fund-raising arm, abstained from voting on the investigation.
An expanded investigation was exactly what Democrats wanted over objections of Republicans who did not want to delve into possibly embarrassing activities involving congressional races.
Agreement on the wider investigation came when Republicans realised they faced an apparent defeat of a plan to just look at "illegal" activities.

By expanding the scope to "improper" as well as illegal, the Senate investigators can look into perfectly legal but questionable unregulated "soft money" donations -- many affecting Republican campaigns as well as Democratic ones.
Democrats argued that inquiring into only illegal activities would leave untouched millions of dollars of unregulated soft money donations.

While donors to individual federal candidates are limited to giving $1,000, donations of any size can go to political parties for party building, get-out-the-vote campaigns and other activities. Republicans traditionally outraise Democrats in so-called soft money.
Republicans said any investigation into "improper" activities should be undertaken by the Senate Rules Committee instead of the Governmental Affairs Committee.
But during a closed-door party luncheon it became clear they were divided on the issue, fearing a perception that they were obstructing a full inquiry.
When the Senate resumed its session, Republican Leader Trent Lott introduced an amendment that would broaden the scope of the investigation to include "improper" activities.
